title: The Danger of Empire
subtitle: Every kingdom that asks you to kneel is asking for something that was never theirs.

sections.kicker: The City That Wanted a Name
sections.title: From Babel to Babylon
sections.body:
The first empire in Scripture begins not with an army but with an ambition. The men of Shinar gather on a plain and say to one another, let us build a city, and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves. That last clause is the whole story. Empire has always been a project of name-making, a way of becoming permanent and feared and unforgettable by stacking enough brick and enough labor and enough bodies into the sky. The tower at Babel is not condemned because building is wicked. It is scattered because the builders wanted to be God, and they wanted to do it together, and they wanted no one to leave.

From that plain the story moves through every imperial form the ancient world could produce. Egypt, where Pharaoh turns a people into a workforce and the cry of the slaves rises up to a God who hears. Assyria, whose kings carved their conquests into stone and bragged about the cities they emptied. Babylon, which carried the southern kingdom into exile and sat down on the throne of the world. The prophets did not flatter any of them. Isaiah mocked the king of Babylon as a falling star. Jeremiah told a generation in chains that the proud city would itself become a heap of ruins where jackals walk.

What unites them is not a flag or a century. It is a posture. Empire is the human refusal to be a creature. It is the determination to make a name that will outlast death by force, to gather the scattered under one tongue and one tax and one fear. Brueggemann called this the royal consciousness, the imagination that cannot picture a world it does not own. The Bible keeps telling the same story because we keep building the same tower.

And we should be honest before we go further. The men of Shinar are not a foreign tribe. They are us, doing the most natural thing in the world, which is to reach for a security that does not depend on God. Babel is not an event in the deep past. It is the standing temptation of every people that grows strong enough to forget it will die.

sections.title: What Empire Always Wants
sections.body:
Strip away the architecture and the propaganda and empire wants one thing. It wants worship. Not always in the religious sense, though often that too. It wants the bent knee, the final loyalty, the place in the heart that belongs to God alone. Every empire eventually builds an image and asks the people to fall down before it, and it is rarely subtle about what happens to those who will not.

The book of Daniel reads like a field manual for this demand. Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden statue on the plain of Dura and orders that when the music plays, everyone falls. Three young men from the exile community decline. Their answer is one of the cleanest lines in the Bible. They tell the king their God is able to deliver them, and then they add, but if not, we still will not serve your gods or worship the image you have set up. But if not. That is the whole resistance compressed into three words. Whether or not we are rescued, you do not get our knee. They go into the furnace and they do not burn.

A generation later the same drama replays with different props. Daniel keeps praying toward Jerusalem after the king signs a law that prayer must be addressed to the king himself for thirty days. He does not protest in the street. He simply keeps his window open and keeps praying, because the alternative is to grant the state a worship it has no right to ask for. He goes into the den of lions and the lions keep their mouths shut. The pattern is fixed and it never changes. Empire offers safety in exchange for ultimate loyalty, and the faithful answer that safety is not worth that price.

Here is the part we would rather skip. The furnace and the den are not only tests for ancient heroes. They are diagnostic tools for us. The question is not whether some distant tyrant would demand my worship. The question is what already has it. What do I trust to keep me safe, to make my name, to tell me who I am. If the honest answer is the nation, or the market, or the movement, then I have already bowed, and no one even had to play the music.

sections.title: Rome and the Cross
sections.body:
When God entered history to deal with empire once and for all, empire killed him. This is not a footnote. The cross is a Roman instrument, designed and perfected by the most efficient imperial machine the world had yet seen, a public technology of terror meant to teach occupied peoples what happens to anyone who imagines an authority above Caesar. Jesus of Nazareth was tried by a Roman governor, mocked with a Roman crown, and nailed up under a Roman charge that named him a rival king. The empire understood the threat better than the disciples did.

The early church understood it too. Rome did not generally care what gods you added to your collection. It cared about one short sentence, the loyalty oath that held the whole world together. Caesar is Lord. The Christians would say almost anything but that. They would care for plague victims the city had abandoned, pay their taxes, pray for the emperor, and then refuse the one confession that would have spared them, because they had already given that word to someone else. Jesus is Lord was not a private comfort. It was a political claim that there is a throne above the throne, and it got people fed to animals in arenas for the entertainment of the very public they were dying to love.

Then came the seduction, and it is the most important turn in this whole history. In 313 the Edict of Milan, issued by Constantine and Licinius, granted toleration to Christians and ended the age of arenas. In 380 the emperor Theodosius went the whole distance, and through the Edict of Thessalonica he made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the empire. Inside that span of two generations the cross had migrated from the thing empire does to its enemies to the thing empire stitches onto its battle standards. The church that would not say Caesar is Lord under threat of death began, under the warmth of imperial favor, to enjoy the proximity to power it had once died to refuse. Cavanaugh names this a migration of the holy, the slow transfer of the devotion once owed to God onto the apparatus of the state, so that the church did not so much conquer the empire as hand the empire its sacred vocabulary and learn to bless the sword instead of suffering under it.

I do not get to read that story from a safe distance. The seduction worked, and it keeps working, because it is pleasant. It is good to be close to power, to be respected by the strong, to have the magistrate on your side. The early church was poor and hunted and clear. We are comfortable and respected and confused. The drift from one to the other did not require anyone to renounce Christ. It only required them to enjoy the favor of empire more than they feared it.

sections.title: The Modern Empires
sections.body:
Empire did not end when the togas went out of fashion. It changed clothes. The form that once wore a crown now wears a flag, a brand, a slogan, an algorithm, and it is far better at hiding because it no longer needs a statue on a plain. It asks for the same knee in subtler language. It still wants to be the thing that makes your name, keeps you safe, and tells you who your enemies are. The modern empire rarely has to threaten anyone with fire. It only has to make the alternative unthinkable.

The nation is the obvious one, and every nation is implicated, including yours and mine. The country that imagines itself uniquely good, uniquely chosen, uniquely entitled to remake the world in its own image, has simply translated Babel into a national anthem. But the nation is no longer the only empire in town. The market is one, training us to believe that our worth is our output and our deepest identity is consumer. The platform is another, a new plain of Shinar where we labor without pay to make a name for ourselves and call the tower freedom. Each one wants the loyalty Daniel would not give the king.

And the temptation is not housed on one side of any argument, which is exactly what each side would like you to believe. The right is tempted to wrap the cross around the nation and baptize its power as the will of God, to mistake a political order for the kingdom. The left is tempted to make a redeemer of the state or the movement, to believe that the right policy and the right coalition will finally heal what is broken in the human heart. Both are forms of empire because both ask an ultimate trust that only God can carry, and both will, when crossed, demand a loyalty that brooks no refusal. The flags differ. The demand for worship does not.

This is where I have to stop pointing. It is easy to see the empire the other tribe has built and almost impossible to see my own, because mine does not feel like empire. It feels like common sense, like the obviously good side, like the people who are simply correct. That is how it always feels from the inside. The men on the plain of Shinar did not think they were rebelling against heaven. They thought they were being reasonable. So do we.

sections.title: The Politics of the Cross
sections.body:
There is a kingdom that does not come the way empires come, and it is the strangest political fact in the world. It does not advance by the sword. It advances by a man on a sword's wrong end. When Peter drew a blade in the garden to defend his king the way every kingdom defends itself, Jesus told him to put it away, and then he let the empire take him. The throne of this kingdom is a Roman cross, and its coronation is an execution, and its triumph looks for three days exactly like a defeat. Empire conquers by making others die. This king conquers by dying.

That is not a strategy empire can copy, because it cannot be faked. You cannot seize power in order to give it away. The cross is the permanent refusal of the imperial logic, the announcement that God's answer to the kingdoms of the world was not a bigger army but an empty tomb, that resurrection is the only victory empire can neither buy nor kill. The early church grasped this and it made them ungovernable in the deepest sense. You cannot finally threaten people who have already died with Christ and been raised. The furnace loses its power over anyone who has stopped trusting it to keep them safe.

So the church is meant to be a different kind of people, not a faction within somebody's empire but a colony of a coming kingdom, a community whose very existence is a quiet argument that the powers are not ultimate. This is not withdrawal and it is not a seat at the table. It is the harder thing of staying near the world's pain while refusing the world's terms, of feeding the hungry without needing the magistrate's permission, of telling the truth when the truth costs the favor we have grown to love. A people who will say of any empire what the three young men said. Maybe you will rescue us and maybe you will not, but we will not bow.

I want to end where this leaves me, and it does not leave me comfortable. The temptation of empire is not a problem for tyrants far away. It is the offer made to me every day, to find my safety and my name and my belonging in something I can see and serve and march behind. The cross asks me to set all of that down and follow a king who won by losing. I would rather have the tower. That is the honest confession, and most days I do not get past it. The empire wants my knee. It was never the empire's to ask for. And the kingdom that does not take it by force asks for the one thing the tower cannot survive my giving away.
